questions.prompt: Given \(|\mathbf a|=6\), \(|\mathbf b|=5\), and angle \(60^\circ\), find \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\).
questions.answer: Use \(|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta\): \(6\cdot5\cdot\cos60^\circ=30\cdot1/2=15\).

questions.prompt: Test whether \((2,1)\) and \((3,-6)\) are perpendicular.
questions.answer: Their dot product is \(2\cdot3+1(-6)=0\). Since both are non-zero, they are perpendicular.

questions.prompt: Find \(|(2,-3,6)|\) using a dot product.
questions.answer: Compute \(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v=4+9+36=49\). Thus \(|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{49}=7\).

questions.prompt: A force \(\mathbf F=(6,2)\) N moves a particle by \(\mathbf s=(3,0)\) m. Find the work done.
questions.answer: Work is \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf s=6\cdot3+2\cdot0=18\) J.

questions.prompt: Find the angle between \((1,0)\) and \((1,1)\).
questions.answer: The dot product is \(1\). The magnitudes are \(1\) and \(\sqrt2\). Thus \(\cos\theta=1/\sqrt2\), so \(\theta=45^\circ\).

questions.prompt: Find the scalar projection of \(\mathbf a=(3,4)\) onto \(\mathbf b=(1,0)\).
questions.answer: Scalar projection is \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b/|\mathbf b|=(3)/1=3\).

questions.prompt: Find the vector projection of \(\mathbf a=(2,3)\) onto \(\mathbf b=(1,1)\).
questions.answer: Use \((\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b/|\mathbf b|^2)\mathbf b\). The factor is \((5)/(2)\), so the projection is \((5/2,5/2)\).
The dot product is \(3k-12\). Set it to zero: \(3k=12\), so \(k=4\).

questions.prompt: Compute \((\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-\mathbf k)\cdot(3\mathbf i-\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)\).
Use dot products to decide whether the triangle with sides \((3,4)\) and \((-4,3)\) at one vertex is right-angled.
questions.answer: Their dot product is \(3(-4)+4(3)=0\), so the sides are perpendicular and the angle is right.

questions.prompt: Find \(\mathbf a\cdot(2\mathbf b-\mathbf c)\) for \(\mathbf a=(1,2)\), \(\mathbf b=(3,0)\), \(\mathbf c=(1,-1)\).
questions.answer: First \(2\mathbf b-\mathbf c=(6,0)-(1,-1)=(5,1)\). Then \(\mathbf a\cdot(5,1)=5+2=7\).

questions.prompt: Find the component of \((4,4)\) in the direction of unit vector \((1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)\).
questions.answer: Dot with the unit vector: \(4/\sqrt2+4/\sqrt2=8/\sqrt2=4\sqrt2\).

questions.prompt: Find the angle between \((1,2,2)\) and \((2,0,1)\).
questions.answer: The dot product is \(4\). The magnitudes are \(3\) and \(\sqrt5\), so \(\cos\theta=4/(3\sqrt5)\). Hence \(\theta=\cos^{-1}(4/(3\sqrt5))\).

questions.prompt: Find \(x\) if \((x,1,2)\) is orthogonal to \((3,-1,4)\).
questions.answer: The dot product is \(3x-1+8=3x+7\). Set it to zero, giving \(x=-7/3\).

questions.prompt: A force of magnitude \(10\) N acts at \(30^\circ\) to a displacement of \(4\) m. Find the work.
questions.answer: Work is \(10\cdot4\cos30^\circ=40(\sqrt3/2)=20\sqrt3\) J.

questions.prompt: Show that \((\mathbf a+\mathbf b)\cdot(\mathbf a-\mathbf b)=|\mathbf a|^2-|\mathbf b|^2\), then explain what happens when \(|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|\).
questions.answer: Expand: \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf a-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a-\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf b\). Since \(\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf a=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\), the middle terms cancel, leaving \(|\mathbf a|^2-|\mathbf b|^2\). If \(|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|\), this value is \(0\), so \(\mathbf a+\mathbf b\) and \(\mathbf a-\mathbf b\) are perpendicular when they are non-zero.

questions.prompt: Find the work done by \(\mathbf F=(2,-1,3)\) along displacement \(\mathbf s=(4,5,-2)\), then find the component of the force in the direction of the displacement.
questions.answer: Work is \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf s=2\cdot4+(-1)5+3(-2)=8-5-6=-3\) J, so the force opposes the displacement overall. The component of force in the displacement direction is \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf s/|\mathbf s|=-3/\sqrt{4^2+5^2+(-2)^2}=-3/(3\sqrt5)=-1/\sqrt5\) N.

questions.prompt: Find \(\lambda\) so that \((1,\lambda,2)\) makes a \(60^\circ\) angle with \((1,0,0)\), with \(\lambda\ge0\).
questions.answer: The dot product is \(1\), and the magnitudes are \(\sqrt{1+\lambda^2+4}\) and \(1\). So \(1/\sqrt{\lambda^2+5}=1/2\). Hence \(\lambda^2+5=4\), impossible, so no such \(\lambda\) exists.
